document.note: Interview with former State Department spokesman and South Asia chief Richard Boucher, obtained by the Washington Post. He says the U.S. did not know what it was doing, went in to get al-Qaeda, then the mission kept expanding ('mission creep'), and the effort to build a centralized state was wrong.

events.description: SIGAR interview of Richard Boucher
US went into Afghanistan to get al-Qaeda out; Taliban fought back and became the enemy
Powell visited Kabul, attended Karzai cabinet meeting
Boucher began his job as Assistant Secretary and visited Kabul and Jalalabad.
Regional economic meeting in India where Boucher gave a three-minute speech on melons.
Opening of US-built Panj bridge with Gutierrez, Karzai and Rahmon.
Powell visit to Kabul and meeting with Karzai's cabinet.
SIGAR Lessons Learned interview with Ambassador Richard Boucher
Boucher wrote a blog post about a 'Sandinista solution' for Syria, about five months before the interview.
Reagan-era pressure led to a negotiated election in Nicaragua, which the Sandinistas lost (Boucher's recollection).
SIGAR Lessons Learned interview with Ambassador Richard Boucher.
Boucher arrives in Afghanistan role as Reach Back Group was on its way out.
US ramps up Afghan police training and sets up electronic payroll after having hardly trained police.
Secretary Powell, Boucher and others visit Kabul; cabinet meeting with Karzai.
Boucher goes to Jalalabad with the DEA Administrator and meets Sherzai, who lists construction needs.
Boucher takes up his post as Assistant Secretary of State and visits Kabul.
Regional economic meeting in India where Boucher spoke about melons from Osh/Fergana reaching New Delhi.
Opening of the US-built bridge across the Panj River between Afghanistan and Tajikistan, attended by Boucher, Gutierrez, Karzai and Rahmon.
US funneled money and weapons via mullahs, military and militant groups in the tribal areas to fight the Soviets, destroying tribal governance structures.
Pakistan nominally retained the tribal-agent payoff system through 2006-2007 before passing insufficient reform laws.
US Special Forces allowed a cross-border ground raid into Pakistan that was described as a fiasco.
Boucher arrives in Afghanistan around 2006-2007; police training and electronic payment system ramped up.
Secretary Powell visits Kabul; attends cabinet meeting with Karzai; embassy toilets get working on the day of visit.
SIGAR Lessons Learned interview of Ambassador Richard Boucher by Matthew Sternenberger and Candace Rondeaux.
US went into Afghanistan to get al-Qaeda; the Taliban fought back and became the enemy.
Boucher traveled to Jalalabad with the DEA Administrator and met Gul Agha Sherzai, who listed his construction needs (5 schools, colleges, dams).
Regional economic cooperation meeting in India at which Boucher gave a short speech about melons from Osh.
Opening of the Panj River bridge between Afghanistan and Tajikistan, attended by Boucher, Gutierrez, Karzai and Rahmon.

key_claims: Boucher says the US did not know what it was doing in Afghanistan; mission creep went from removing al-Qaeda to ending the Taliban to building a stable government.
Boucher argues aid was mostly spent through US contractors, so only 10-20% reached Afghanistan and under 10% a village.
Boucher says Karzai ruled by relying on friends and provincial powerbrokers rather than the bureaucratic structure the US imposed.
Boucher blames Rumsfeld's light-footprint approach and the shift to Iraq for neglecting Afghan police training.
Boucher says the lead-nation sector approach (Germans police, Italians justice) failed.
Boucher says US 1980s funding of mullahs, military and militant groups created a mullah-military-militant complex that destroyed tribal governing structures in Pakistan's tribal areas.
Boucher cites Haqqani as an example of a militant leader whose authority derived from the war against the Soviets.
Boucher believes the Pakistani military was expected to take care of the militant problem for the US, with limited cross-border coordination that failed.
Boucher suggests allegations that some US aid reached the Taliban by fairly direct means were probably true.
Boucher says the lead-nation sector approach (Germans police, Italians justice) failed and that Karzai was imposed without Afghans organizing themselves.
Boucher says Uzbek militants and Uighurs with the Taliban and al-Qaeda were shared concerns with Central Asian states and China.
Boucher says Rahmon's request for rail to Iran made strategic sense but was politically and practically impossible given US sanctions on Iran.
Boucher argues de-Ba'athification in Iraq offers lessons for Syria more than for Afghanistan, since Afghanistan lacked a functioning state core.
Boucher says removing secular dictators (Tito, Saddam, Gaddafi, Assad) produces sectarian violence.
Boucher advocates a balance of one-third military, one-third regional players, one-third governance.
Boucher lists lessons including lowering expectations, defining goals, avoiding mission creep, and building 'decent' governance as an exit strategy.
